speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Government has strengthened our systems over the years to enhance access to justice for Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents (PRs).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This includes working with the Judiciary to enhance and improve Court processes to save time and costs and enhancing frameworks to enable Singaporeans to resolve their disputes quickly in a cost-effective manner, such as through the use of mediation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Even with various Government-driven initiatives to reduce the costs of dispute resolution, we recognise that some in our society may still be unable to afford their own lawyers for basic legal services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Providing access to justice to persons of limited means underpins the Legal Aid and Advice Act, and the establishment of the Legal Aid Bureau (LAB).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: To ensure that public funds are properly allocated to the most vulnerable persons who have reasonable grounds for legal proceedings they wish to pursue, the Act currently has a two-fold test for legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, applicants must satisfy the means criteria based on the applicants’ disposable income and disposable capital.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, applicants must then pass a merits test.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Government regularly reviews the Act to ensure that the Act remains able to meet the objectives that I have just set out.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This facilitates the modification and simplification of the means criteria.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, the means criteria involve an assessment of disposable income and disposable capital.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Disposable income is calculated by taking the total income of the applicant and his or her spouse and deducting various permitted deductibles, such as living allowances and Central Provident Fund (CPF) contributions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Disposable capital is calculated by taking the value of the property which an applicant possesses or is entitled to and deducting various permitted deductibles, such as a Housing and Development Board (HDB) flat owned and used by the applicant and his family as their home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These criteria have worked well to identify those who have a real need for legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Nevertheless, some changes to the means criteria may better serve the most vulnerable in the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill will allow us to provide for means criteria to be set out in subsidiary legislation, and we intend to simplify the means criteria, without compromising on its effectiveness at identifying the truly needy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The new means criteria will involve assessing the applicant's gross income and assets, instead of his disposable income and disposable capital.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This also simplifies the application process for legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The new means criteria will be set such that there will be no material impact on the number of households which will remain eligible for legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We will continue to regularly monitor and review the new means criteria after implementation to ensure that legal aid remains available to persons of limited means.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Other than simplifying the means criteria, the Bill also provides greater flexibility for legal aid to be given where it is just and proper to do so, for example, to those who may find themselves in extenuating circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This can be found in clause 7(b) of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, the Act only allows for a limited deviation from the means criteria.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: To illustrate, the Director of Legal Aid may disregard certain matters in determining the disposable income and disposable capital of an applicant in four specific circumstances defined in the Second Schedule.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Those circumstances can be broadly summarised as follows: One, where the applicant lives apart from his or her spouse.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Two, where the applicant has a sudden physical or mental disability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Three, where the applicant has a sudden loss of income.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: And four, where the applicant is involved in certain family proceedings involving children, or protection orders between spouses or ex-spouses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In computing the applicant’s disposable income or disposable capital, the Director may: (a) grant such applicants additional deductibles; or (b) exclude the income of the applicant’s spouse.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, the Act restricts how much the Director can do in these situations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It also does not allow the means criteria to be adjusted for other applicants who might otherwise fail the means criteria but do not fall within any of those four categories.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We understand that applicants may sometimes need more help.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Applicants with other circumstances not currently prescribed in the Act may also face other strains on their financial resources and they may not be able to afford legal fees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For example, LAB currently is unable to help an applicant who fails the means criteria but cannot afford legal services because he has a sudden serious illness and has to pay for major medical procedures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill will provide greater flexibility for LAB to assist these applicants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Minister may also authorise any person, including a panel of persons, to exercise this power.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The remainder of the Bill makes general improvements to the administration of legal aid, and I will run through a few of the more significant provisions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 3 empowers the Director to appoint public officers to assist the Director, the Deputy Director or the Assistant Director of Legal Aid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: They will first undergo rigorous and specialised training for this purpose.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 7(a) also empowers the Director to decide on the merits test in certain proceedings, instead of referring the matter to a board which comprises the Director and no fewer than two solicitors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is to streamline the merits test process for what could be straightforward cases, such as uncontested divorce cases where the parties have agreed on all related or ancillary matters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, they may only obtain a copy of the judge's Notes of Evidence free of charge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The additional documents, such as Grounds of Decision or certified transcripts in relation to proceedings for which legal aid is granted, will be set out in the subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: At present, it is envisaged that contributions may have to be paid where legal advice and assistance in preparing certain legal documents is requested.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We do not intend to charge a contribution for applicants who have received only oral legal advice, as is the current practice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It facilitates the simplification of the means criteria for applicants, provides more flexibility for legal aid to be granted where just and proper, and overall improves on the administration of legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill reaffirms the Government’s commitment to ensure access to justice for the most vulnerable, and I trust these changes will also enhance LAB’s ability to do its work in the many years to come.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Often times, a person may feel daunted by the prospect of needing to navigate the legal process on one’s own.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some knowledge of the law may be needed to make legal arguments in Court.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some may not be able to afford Court fees, let alone hire legal assistance, aid or representation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For justice to be administered, the best institutional and legal infrastructure is necessary but insufficient; access to them is also important.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At this juncture, I should declare that I am a lawyer in private practice.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Access to justice is important, not just for justice between relevant parties, but is also critical for society, a rule of law society, a society where people obey the law and are guided by the law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As an example, if an employer knew that he or she can get away with not paying the employee's wages agreed upon in the contract because the employee is unable to bring a claim against him or her, it would be much easier for an employer to unlawfully withhold wages.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But this would not be the case if the employer knew the employee has access to justice.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, by knowing that there is a possibility that the Court system may be utilised to enforce the claim, there will be greater incentive to obey the law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this way, access to justice promotes the rule of law, even before something goes wrong.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, in certain circumstances, when something goes wrong, access to justice is important for people to not feel that they need to take things into their own hands by resorting to violence, for instance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A tangible example of this is personal protection orders, one of the many things that LAB helps its clients with.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Through this Bill, LAB will be even more effective in its mission of advancing access to justice and the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I should also state that many members of the Singapore Bar already provide hours upon hours of pro bono services to clients who cannot afford legal fees.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, these amendments in this Bill should be viewed as complementing the already selfless effort of many members of the litigation Bar.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This simplifies the process and makes it easier for applicants who need various forms of help to use the same supporting documents to apply for the different kinds of help.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Related to this, would the Senior Minister of State elaborate on how the qualifying limit will be set?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On a related note, there is an increased discretion for the Minister to direct the Director to accept deserving cases should the applicant not meet the rigid means test.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The broadened discretion expands the discretion beyond just loss of income or loss of earning capacity, to, for instance, a person who cannot afford legal services because he needs to pay for major medical procedures due to a serious illness.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As difficulties in life that may reduce one's ability to afford legal assistance are very varied, it is good that there is greater discretion.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Minister elaborate on how this discretion is to be exercised?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Is the aim to help those with around the same needs profile as those under the strict means test even though the need may arise from different circumstances?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill also enables LAB to better manage their resources.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Under clause 3, the Director may appoint someone who is not a qualified person under the Legal Profession Act to appear and plead in Court for an aided person.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Minister elaborate on the rigorous training that these public officers will undergo so that LAB will continue to be known for its high-quality legal services and so LAB’s clients' interests can continue to be effectively represented?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Notwithstanding the ability to appoint public officers to represent clients, Assigned Solicitors continue to play an important role in the LAB's work.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, they still seem necessary for specialised cases involving medical negligence, Syariah Court cases, or where both parties applied for legal aid.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Under clause 4, Assigned Solicitors serve for terms of approximately three years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a welcome move, especially because other Court documents may be necessary in the civil process.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, the record of proceedings in a notice of appeal includes a certified copy of the grounds of judgment or order, if any, and a copy of the certified transcript of the official record of the hearing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In strengthening access to justice, this Bill also advances the rule of law in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The update and simplification of the means criteria for legal aid to align them with means criteria used in current social support schemes have been long-awaited.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To apply for legal aid today, applicants have to furnish documentary proof of their disposable income and disposable capital as part of the legal aid application.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The incidence of abuse is low and the large majority of applicants meet the qualifying criteria.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In 2016, 57% of the legal aid applicants had only secondary educational qualifications or lower.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The challenges that this group face in accessing justice are multifold.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, with lower educational levels, they will meet with more challenges in understanding their legal rights, seeking available recourse and comprehending legal processes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, with limited financial means, there are significant financial challenges in seeking legal recourse.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, the inability or difficulty faced in seeking legal recourse can exacerbate existing challenges in their lives due to higher levels of stress arising from the inability to resolve the legal issue at hand.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: When divorce is on the cards, there would inevitably be strain in the household.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The parties involved and their family and children bear the emotional cost of the dragging out of a failing relationship.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The ability to seek legal recourse, especially in cases where violence is perpetuated, must be available in the legal system and accessible.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There must also be urgency in helping lower-income claimants recover monies owing to them, and assistance for lower-income families who have lost a loved one to unlock assets of the deceased, especially where the deceased was the breadwinner.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The mission of LAB is about "Advancing access to justice, the rule of law, the economy and society through policy, law and services." The amendments proposed under this Bill, indeed, further this mission.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is also timely at this juncture to consider a more integrated approach to provide more holistic support to families which are in need.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Legal issues are not merely disputes between litigant and defendant; they can have extenuating and longer-term impact on the family.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To help families to manage stress arising from the legal dispute and any potential fallout, they can be directed to counselling support.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Households in need can be directed to social assistance schemes and employment facilitation services.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At the close of the claim, a review should also be conducted to educate vulnerable claimants on how to better protect their legal rights in future.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Hon Deputy Speaker and hon Members, Singaporeans may not often talk about justice, but few will doubt how important it is to have recourse to the law to affirm one’s rights; or to receive proper compensation for one’s work; or to protect one’s property; or to receive a fair arrangement at the end of a marriage; or to obtain protection from abuse.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In our pledge, we refer to ourselves as a society based on justice and equality.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: To realise that pledge, I believe that justice may be accessible to anyone who seeks it or who requires it.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: That is why I support this Bill as it is a great step towards strengthening access to justice for Singaporeans who may not ordinarily be able to afford lawyers or seek legal help.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to zoom in on two areas: Public Awareness of Legal Aid and Expanding Services.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It will also align the means criteria to what is commonly used in other social support schemes.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I also support the move for greater discretion in the granting of legal aid.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: There are many applicants who are truly needy and deserving but find themselves unable to meet the means criteria for whatever reasons.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: A closer scrutiny of these cases and an inclusive approach are welcome.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The recent announcement of a website revamp at the LAB's 60th anniversary dinner is another step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I support the digitisation of the registration and document submission process as it will help speed up the process to match assigned solicitors to those who are seeking legal aid.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: But based on my interactions with Singaporeans through my outreach work with Roses of Peace, it seems that there are still Singaporeans who may not be aware of the available avenues for legal assistance like LAB or the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS), despite efforts by the Ministry as well as legal awareness campaigns by the Law Society of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I would like to ask the Minister if there are any more steps that can be taken to educate the public, especially those who require legal assistance but are unable to afford it, about the legal help that is available to the public.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps our civil society and our social service organisations can play a part to help spread the word on the avenues available for legal help.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I note that Singaporeans who are receiving financial assistance from our various social support systems may also often require access to legal aid.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: However, not all the frontline officers providing assistance to these individuals and their families may be equipped with the right knowledge of our legal aid services.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, we can have a Legal Aid Conference to inform and equip these frontline officers from the social sector with basic legal knowledge and information on legal aid so that they can help their beneficiaries.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It will also be of great benefit to have a legal aid playbook or an online resource guide that can be accessed by the public.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Most were for matrimonial, claims and probate matters.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I also support the increased funding and support for the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS) over the past years.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: These are important institutions in the provision of legal aid and access to justice.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: But the public often turn to LAB when it is too late, when issues have come to a head or a problem has arisen.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, there is a role that can be played in promoting awareness of the law and to equip the public with enough legal knowledge in order to prevent legal issues from occurring.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: For example, in the area of promoting micro enterprises among low-income families, LAB or the Law Society of Singapore's Pro Bono Services Office can explore working with community organisations, such as Casa Raudha, the Singapore Muslim Women’s Association (PPIS) and Daughters of Tomorrow (DOT), or our trade associations and chambers of commerce, and even small and medium enterprises (SME) Centres, to equip them with legal resources that can help micro enterprises.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In the example of DOT, it is a registered charity that aims to facilitate livelihood opportunities for underprivileged women to build and sustain financially independent and resilient families.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: They have to juggle between caring for their children and making ends meet through their micro enterprises.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Equipping organisations, such as DOT with the right legal resources, such as business contract templates and other relevant knowledge, will go a long way to assist these women and, hopefully, prevent legal issues from occurring, thus, reducing the need for legal aid in a small but important and significant manner.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It is a sign of a compassionate society when we ensure that even those who lack financial means may still be able to afford the ability to protect his or her rights.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Access to justice provides all Singaporeans with the same dignity and the same fundamental right to fairness.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many Members, myself included, have asked for the Director of Legal Aid to be given broader discretion to extend legal aid to those who do not qualify under the means test.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These legislative amendments, coupled with improvements in implementation, are progressive moves towards improving access to justice for the most vulnerable and our becoming a more compassionate society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, if legal costs have increased, access to lawyers may be beyond the reach to a larger number of households.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If that is the case, rather than holding the number of eligible households constant, legal aid may need to be extended to a larger number of households.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The last large-scale study of legal costs in Singapore was the 2001 Census of the Legal Industry and Profession.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The census had suggested that the billable rate of law firms had steadily increased between 1998 and 2000.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Ministry consider increasing the percentage of qualifying citizens and PRs?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, currently, an aided person who wishes to appeal a decision must make a new application for legal aid.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the Assigned Solicitor's Guide, the solicitor is advised that they cannot act for an aided person who is looking to appeal a Court judgment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are strict timelines that must be adhered to in an appeal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is acknowledged in the Assigned Solicitor's Guide, which advises the aided person to file a Notice of Appeal on their own before making a new application for legal aid.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, whether the aided person decides to appeal is likely to depend on whether they are able to obtain further legal aid.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this situation, it is left to the Assigned Solicitor to decide on their own initiative whether to assist the aided person in filing the Notice of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Could the Minister clarify the rationale for subjecting the aided person to another round of means and merits testing to obtain legal aid for the appeal?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The means of the aided person might have changed, but I doubt it would have changed significantly for most persons.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Admittedly, the merits of the case may need to be considered afresh if it is going to an appeal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: An unfavourable decision may cast new light on the merits of the claim.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In a favourable decision where the aided person is appealing against the amount awarded, it should be considered whether the sum awarded truly is so unsatisfactory as to warrant an appeal and whether this should be supported with legal aid.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, given that the claim has gone through an initial round of merits testing, it may not need the in-depth assessment given to a new claim.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Similarly, a new application for legal aid must be made for an aided person to enforce the judgment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Could the Minister also clarify the rationale for subjecting the aided person to another full round of means and merits testing to obtain legal aid in enforcing the judgment?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The means of an aided person would similarly not have changed much after obtaining the paper judgment from the Court.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The merits of the case would be further reinforced by the favourable judgment given by the Court.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Having supported an aided person all the way to the point of obtaining a paper judgment, surely it would be logical for Legal Aid to see the claim all the way through until the aided person obtains the sum claimed, which is the entire objective of filing a claim in the first place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would the Minister consider allowing an initial Grant of Aid to extend to enforcement processes that an aided person may need to undertake?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, the new set of criteria still leaves certain applicants at a disadvantage.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Ministry will be able to exercise some flexibility for such applicants on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will it be considered a component of savings and investments?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If so, can it be excluded since the payouts from CPF are not immediate?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can this be taken into consideration for his application?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What were the main reasons for the unsuccessful applications?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Ministry provide details of the various categories?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, for applicants rejected for legal aid, can the Ministry consider alternative assistance for them?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, I conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I welcome these landmark amendments proposed to the Legal Aid and Advice Act which comes 62 years after the enactment of the original Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The raison d’etre behind the Bill when it was moved by the then Minister for Labour, Mr Lim Yew Hock, in 1956 remains the same.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This point was put across eloquently by the hon Minister Ms Indranee Rajah in this House in 2013 when she said, "Access to justice is one of the cornerstones of our society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We may have the best laws, the best Courts and the best system, but all that would be lost if they cannot be accessed by persons in need.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Like all things, there is a cost to legal services and not everyone can afford such services.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It was with this in mind that the Legal Aid and Advice Act was originally enacted in 1956 to ensure access to justice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That objective remains as relevant today as it was then".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have just heard the Senior Minister of State, Mr Edwin Tong, subscribing fully to this statement and the hon Member Mr Abbas Ali also echoed a similar point.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When the LAB was established pursuant to the Act on 1 July 1958, Singapore became the first country in Southeast Asia to have such a legal aid scheme.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Currently, LAB sees over 9,000 applications for legal aid annually.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is timely that we review our legal aid scheme to ensure that we keep abreast with changes to our society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I recognise that it is not easy to fix a fair and equitable means test that is totally immune to criticism.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The new means criterion of PCHI is commendable, as it allows more flexibility in the assessment of means, to take into account the overall income situation of the household and not the applicant's individual situation, which may not be reflective of his/her situation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Last month, I filed a Parliamentary Question arising from a case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It concerned a legal aid application made by a father, seeking assistance to be appointed as a deputy of his mentally disabled son.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I asked why is it that the father was treated as the applicant as opposed to the son.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Ordinarily, his son would have been eligible for legal aid.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But he cannot apply because he is not mentally capable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The application for deputyship and legal aid was made by the father.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The application, after all, was for the benefit of the son and it was meant to facilitate the care and management of his son.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Unfortunately, the father was deemed not eligible for legal aid, as the current means test only looks at his circumstances as an individual and not that of his son.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under the Act, the Director of Legal Aid may exercise discretion to exclude up to $30,000 to determine the disposable capital of the applicant if the applicant is suffering from mental disability, a point that the learned Senior Minister of State just made.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But here, this ground cannot be raised because, as far as LAB is concerned, the applicant is the father, who is mentally sound.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, one wonders when this proviso can apply because, ordinarily, one assumes that applicants must be compos mentis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In his reply, the Minister for Law stated, "It is not possible for legal aid applications to be made for, or on behalf of, the mentally incapacitated person, and then use that person's means to support the legal aid application".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The means test must be flexible enough to remain relevant even when there are ups and downs in Singapore's economic growth.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In terms of the qualifying limit for the new PCHI means criterion, which I understand will be set later in subsidiary legislation after taking into account the latest income data, could the hon Senior Minister of State please elaborate what are the considerations that will be inputted in relation to setting the limit?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, would it be based on the 20th percentile of the PCHI?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would the income limit exclude CPF contributions, a point that the hon Member Mr Gan Thiam Poh mentioned?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This should be the case, in my respectful view, because it should take into account actual disposable income.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How about circumstances where families are put into significant expense?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I believe that the Senior Minister of State mentioned that this would be taken into account.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What will be the principles governing such assessments?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is presumably so, because the Director would have already made an assessment of eligibility at the first instance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If so, would the Minister require the Director to provide grounds for his decision and would such grounds be provided to the applicant so that the applicant can comment on it in its appeal to the Minister?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And what are circumstances that are contemplated where it would be "just and proper" for the Minister to grant legal aid?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At that point in time, I read the Hansard and it was indicated that the Ministry would consider the suggestion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would be grateful for an update, please.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Over 60 years, the views expressed in this House is consistently that justice must be accessible to all.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Allow me to begin my speech in Malay.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   One of the key principles of our legal framework in Singapore is access to justice.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This means that one should have the right to obtain legal advice and present one’s case in Court regardless of social standing or financial ability.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This right should not be hampered by high legal costs or complex administrative processes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Therefore, efforts must always be made to ensure that support is available to those who require legal aid.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In Singapore, we have legal clinics, where the public can access general legal aid for free.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have the LAB that can provide assistance for civil cases like divorce cases and there is also CLAS for criminal cases.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I also know of lawyers who sometimes would do pro bono or low bono work to help their clients who may have difficulties in paying the full legal costs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The types of assistance I mentioned earlier have more or less helped to address concerns about the issue of access to legal aid.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, there are existing challenges that deserve some attention.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Today, we are debating specifically on the Bill for legal aid and advice that will form an administrative guide for LAB, which handles legal aid for civil cases.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One of the concerns often raised is the process of means-testing someone before legal aid can be provided by LAB.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Currently, when applying for legal aid, there are numerous details that must be provided and documents to prepare.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It also takes time and causes the means-testing process to be further delayed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is hoped that with these new criteria, the application process can be shortened.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I also hope that the criteria that will be established can be scrutinised so that more people can be helped.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On this note, another matter that is often raised is the eligibility for legal aid.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Having legal troubles is not something one often plans for or expects.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So, when one needs to commence action or defend a case in Court, he or she may face difficulties financing the legal costs, even though he or she may be earning a decent income.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Certainly, there should be guidelines for the proper exercise of this discretion.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am hopeful that this discretion will be used judiciously and can benefit more people who may be going through a difficult time in their lives.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English): Access to justice, regardless of social standing or financial ability, is a cornerstone of our legal framework in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Efforts must be made to overcome issues of cost, delay or complexities of the legal system that may hinder access to legal advice or the ability to present one's case in Court.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In Singapore, we have legal clinics, the LAB and CLAS to partly address the need for access to justice.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I also know of lawyers who would do pro bono or low bono work to assist clients who may not be able to afford legal costs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, there are existing challenges within the current framework in the provision of legal aid and advice.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Therefore, this Bill is a welcome move and the opportunity to discuss this matter today is much appreciated.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One of the issues often raised is the means-testing process that is currently in place.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The assessment process calls for much information and numerous documents to be provided.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This can be overwhelming and daunting for the applicant.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At a time when they most need help and are most likely preoccupied with significant matters happening in their lives, the requirement to prepare copious documents before they can get help, adds to the stress.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: While I understand the need for alignment, there are already concerns with the existing means criteria.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For example, in determining PCHI, we have heard some grievances of those who have children or relations living in the same address but not contributing to the household income.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Also, in considering the AV of a property, it would be pertinent to note that there may be people who are residing in a private property not as a luxury but because of their circumstances.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These grievances may be adopted if we take the PCHI and AV assessment methods wholesale.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Would there be some way of addressing some of these issues head-on and provide for appropriate deductions or exceptions at the outset?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am not suggesting that the assessments are made less rigorous.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe it is important to check properly and only grant aid to those who truly deserve it.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, if we already know that the applicant may be facing some difficulties, perhaps we could account for these situations, subject to the provision of some basic evidence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The other issue that is often raised as a pain point is the eligibility for legal aid.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Could there be adjustments to the limits of the prescribed means test to allow for more to qualify for legal aid?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Having legal troubles is not something one often plans for or expects.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is not a habit to set aside savings for legal costs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So, when there is a need to commence an action or defend a case in Court, it is common to hear of situations where the individual is financially stretched and has difficulties financing his or her legal costs, even though he or she may be earning a decent income.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In recent times, there have been calls for more legal assistance to be given to the sandwich class.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I appreciate that a line has to be drawn somewhere and we will not be able to help everyone.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe there will be guidelines for the proper exercise of this discretion.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am hopeful that this discretion would allow for more deserving applicants to receive help even though they may not meet all the prescribed means requirements.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On a separate note, in the effort to enhance access to justice and close the gaps, I believe one strategy is to encourage and incentivise low pro bono efforts by lawyers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have already many lawyers doing pro bono work.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But this often comes at a cost to the lawyer’s earnings.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I know people joke about how much a lawyer earns.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But the truth is that not all lawyers are mercenary and not all lawyers earn big profits.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A law practice is also a business and would have overheads and operational costs, just like a medical practice or other professional services.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In fact, the legal fraternity also has to go through industry transformation like other industries in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Bearing this in mind, and considering the need to close some gaps, we may, therefore, want to cast our sights on a more sustainable solution which could be a win-win solution for all.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I hope there would be more support in thinking about and developing such low bono models that could allow for more to benefit from getting proper legal advice and aid, but which could also support the legal sector.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I would like MinLaw to clarify about four points.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Can I understand more about how Legal Aid will determine what kind of processes or cases will merit public officers rather than qualified persons?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Are all PRs given the same rights as Singapore Citizens with regard to legal aid?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Or is there another set of tighter criteria necessary for PRs to qualify, such as closer ties to Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Can MinLaw share the rationale of this change?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: How can we balance achieving this potential increased efficiency with the downside of having the Director being a bottleneck or a single point of failure?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Last of all, can MinLaw share about how LAB assesses financial criteria on who to help, especially on the grounds of discretion?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, there are some families with higher income than the threshold, but the family relationship may have been strained and money is not allowed, or the family have significant medical expenses or debts.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Another point we could look at is the cost of the legal aid to be provided.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I mean, say, for example, the sandwich class.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: One is to get LAB to handle something that costs thousands of dollars of legal fees.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding my queries, I support the amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I also thank the very many volunteer lawyers, pro bono lawyers like Mr Murali Pillai who is an Assigned Solicitor for LAB, because these people, apart from the rules and regulations that we make, these lawyers, with their pro bono work, contribute to the richness of making justice accessible to even the most disadvantaged in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are several queries on the Bill and I would like to jump straight into addressing them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about the number of legal aid applications.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In general, applicants who were unsuccessful had failed the eligibility criteria because they exceeded the disposable income or capital assets limit.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Around half of LAB’s cases concern matrimonial matters.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Other common cases concern the enforcement of Court orders, monetary disputes and also probate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Henry Kwek asked about the assessment, while Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Murali Pillai asked about the qualifying limits and how they would be set.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked whether CPF moneys would be included in the assessment of the applicant’s savings and investments, and Mr Murali Pillai also asked whether CPF contributions would be included in the assessment of the applicant’s income.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The new criteria are simpler and much more aligned with what are commonly used in current social support schemes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The new means criteria consider the applicant's gross income and assets, instead of his disposable income and disposable capital.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will incorporate most of the permitted deductibles within the current means criteria, such as CPF contributions, when setting the new income limits in the new assessment criteria to minimise the risk that those applicants who were previously eligible would no longer be eligible when we move from disposable income to gross income.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will not include the applicant's CPF moneys in the computation of the applicant’s savings and investments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is also consistent with our existing means test.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, we do not anticipate at this point in time a significant spike in the number of cases that come forward, and, hence, my point earlier about the allocation of Government resources.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: My Ministry will allocate the appropriate resources to deal with any increased caseload as they arise.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But bear in mind also that the amendments do provide for Specialist Legal Executives to come on board to lend support to the giving of advice and also to appear in Court for some of these cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, that will also ease the load on LAB.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked if the use of household income would disadvantage applicants who need to support family members staying in a different household.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other words, what Mr Gan is saying is that if I look at only the household income of this individual, it may not give me a full picture because he may be supporting a family member residing in a different household.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We do not consider family members living in a different household in calculating the PCHI because family relationships can be complex and diverse.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The situation that Mr Gan Thiam Poh cited could well work the other way, where an applicant could be supported by a family member not living in the same household.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other words, he is coming to apply, and based on his PCHI, he would qualify, but yet, he is also being supported by a family member living outside of his household.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Government is not privy to the family dynamics in each situation and so, it is best at this stage to use the household income as the best proxy for family support.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Furthermore, this will also be more convenient for applicants, as they will not have to provide information on family members who may not live with them, the extent of their support and the extent of their familial relationship, and why that may be.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, at present, we will keep to using the PCHI.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Given these, we will adopt PCHI as I said, although I would stress that, in appropriate cases, we would also be able to consider the scenario that Mr Gan Thiam Poh mentioned, where it is just and proper to do so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is precisely the reason for the framework that we are building into the new amendments, where if it is just and proper, then the Minister may have the discretion to allow aid to be granted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To take the example a bit further, if the applicant is the sole source of support for that family member, and the family member is not a beneficiary of other Government schemes, those are factors that can be taken into account.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng had asked whether the Ministry is tracking the legal costs and the proportion of households for whom legal representation remains accessible and whether we would consider increasing the coverage for civil legal aid.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam also asked if there could be adjustments to the limits to allow for more to qualify for legal aid.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would assure Members that MinLaw regularly reviews the means test for civil legal aid, taking into account legal costs, the cost of living and other factors, to ensure that legal aid remains accessible to Singapore Citizens and also PRs of limited means who cannot afford their own lawyers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Legal aid is targeted and given only to those with limited means, as it has to be, because we have limited resources and we need to be prudent about how we allocate them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked if we could consider negative net worth as part of the means assessment, if the applicant's debt liabilities exceed his assets.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think what Mr Gan Thiam Poh has in mind is that if you are servicing or have taken out a loan which may be secured and where the security value may be below the value of the loan that has been taken, whether that can be taken into account.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The reason we do not do that is because the applicant may have secured debt liabilities, for example, a mortgage or a car loan, which is quite common, but may still possess savings or income above the means limits.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This may then allow him to afford legal fees.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will also consider an indebted individual with extenuating circumstances on a case-by-case basis, and may grant aid where it is just and proper to do so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, if the debt was incurred due to a significant expense as a result of an intervening event, as Mr Murali Pillai puts it, for example, a serious acute medical condition, then yes, those are circumstances that will be taken into account as well in the assessment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And this will allow us to provide aid in a more targeted manner, which would also achieve greater equity.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This brings me to the questions from Mr Christopher de Souza, Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Murali Pillai who asked how this flexibility could be exercised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali asked, in particular, what are the circumstances where it would be "just and proper" to grant aid.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I have given a sense of what that might be in my earlier paragraph.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Rahayu also asked if we can consider extenuating circumstances, for example, children or relatives staying in the same household but not contributing to the household income, or applicants who stay in private properties due to their circumstances, in our computation of PCHI or AV.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The intention behind the amendments and the regime that has been set in place with the amendments in this Bill is, of course, to allow for a more flexible assessment to be made in order that aid can be granted if the Minister is of the opinion that it would be just and proper to do so, the key words being "just and proper".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We want to retain that flexibility on a case-by-case basis, because each case will be different; the circumstances present for each applicant will be different and we want to have the flexibility to be able to assess these factors on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When such cases arise, the Minister may authorise any person, and that includes a panel of persons, suitably qualified, to make that assessment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In exercising the discretion, we may consider granting aid to an applicant who might otherwise fail the means criteria but still not be able to afford legal services due to extenuating circumstances, such as those that Members had mentioned.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai gave some examples and Ms Rahayu Mahzam as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will also consider if family members staying in the same household cannot contribute to the individual’s legal costs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Children are one example; the other would be where the family members living in the same household may be estranged from one another.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I just do not want to be taken in my answer to be limiting the circumstances which we consider.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, I do stress that it is on a case-by-case basis and looking at the particular facts of each case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Applicants who fail the means criteria will be informed of the reason.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Applicants who may then have extenuating circumstances can bring this up to the Minister, under the procedure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At this point in time, we are working out the operational details and also the procedural steps necessary for this to be highlighted, but it will not be treated as a statutory appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked if the Ministry can consider alternative sources of assistance to applicants who do not qualify for legal aid, in other words, persons who fail the means test.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And the example Mr Gan Thiam Poh gave was to ask solicitors to grant a deferred payment scheme for legal fees.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Government assistance is generally given to those most vulnerable and those most in need of assistance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And that is what the current regime for means criteria seeks to achieve.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If an applicant satisfies these criteria, plus the merits test, he will be given legal aid.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But if the applicant does not satisfy the criteria, but goes on, nonetheless, to engage a lawyer, we will be unable to mandate that there be a deferred payment scheme for such services, which are really between the individual as the client, and his solicitor.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But this, not being able to do it by legislation, does not stop a client from requesting his lawyers to consider either an instalment scheme or a deferred payment scheme as may be appropriate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, we will also be making various improvements to the administration of legal aid.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked for an elaboration of the rigorous training that public officers who are not qualified persons under the Legal Profession Act will undergo in order to appear and plead in Court for an aided person.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Henry Kwek asked if MinLaw would decide what cases these public officers would take on and whether this would compromise the interest of aided persons.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: LAB will ensure the thorough and proper training of such persons and will ensure that no aided person’s interest will be compromised as a result of the use of such public officers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: LAB's Legal Executives are well-trained and they complement the work of Legal Officers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Currently, Legal Executives already perform a significant amount of work at LAB and this includes the taking of instructions and preparing drafts of certain documents.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All appointed Specialist Legal Executives will have to attend legal knowledge courses on relevant subject areas to the kind of work that they do.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it would be in areas of divorce, mediation, the Singapore Legal System, professional skills and, of course, legal writing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These courses will be provided by both external providers, as well as through the inhouse legal expertise which already exists at LAB.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They will have to go through a practical training programme, which will cover skills, such as drafting, client-management, client-facing work, Court etiquette and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They will be accompanied and receive inhouse supervision by experienced legal officers and have assessments made, before they are allowed to attend Court and represent clients.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This training will ensure that the Specialist Legal Executives will be well-equipped to handle the expanded scope of work so that LAB’s clients’ interests will be effectively represented.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If the matters that these officers are handling become subsequently contested or more challenging, they will be handed over to a lawyer, who will take over the matter.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will continually review the role of the Specialist Legal Executive to consider what more they can do.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will, no doubt, ease the burden and bring down costs overall as well as allow for cases to be managed more expeditiously, as I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Henry Kwek asked about the rationale for allowing the Director, instead of the Legal Aid Board, to grant aid for straightforward matters.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Kwek asked if we could avoid the Director being a "bottleneck".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Currently, at this point in time, the merits of all applications are assessed by the Legal Aid Board which comprises the Director of Legal Aid and not fewer than two solicitors from a panel of solicitors maintained under the Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This means that after LAB has prepared a legal opinion for an applicant, the applicant may have to wait for up to two weeks before aid is granted, deferred or refused.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The discretion, however, will only be exercised in straightforward matters, such as uncontested matters relating to Probate, Letters of Administration and Guardianship matters where the defendants consent to the proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Any application for which aid may be refused will still go through the Legal Aid Board.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Henry Kwek asked whether PRs would be subject to a more stringent set of criteria in our assessment on whether they qualify for civil legal aid.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng asked why aided persons have to go through a fresh means test when appealing a decision for a case in which aid was previously granted and for a case where the aided person subsequently wishes to enforce the judgment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked whether the Minister would consider an expedited process for assessing whether to extend aid to an aided person who wishes to file an appeal, given that strict timelines do apply in the context of when an appeal is brought.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We require aided persons to go through a fresh means and merits test because considerable time may have elapsed between the time that the person first applied for legal aid and it was granted, and the completion of his initial matter.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The means may have changed during this period of time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And, as Mr Louis Ng also acknowledged, the merits may also have changed, given that the proceedings have taken place, evidence may have been led, and a judgment may have been issued on the case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, a fresh merits test is also necessary to ensure that we continue to grant aid only to those most deserving and this includes those who are applying for or seeking a meritorious outcome, and this includes for an appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: No doubt when a second merits test is involved, where one is making an assessment on the same matter after some time has elapsed, the time taken for that assessment will be quicker.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This Grant is typically valid for a period of three months and can be further extended if necessary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Under the Provisional Grant of Aid, the Bureau may assist the aided person with the filing of the Notice of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, the Director can also issue a notification under section 17 of the Legal Aid and Advice Act to stay the proceedings for a period of 14 days, whilst this is being done.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked if the Ministry has considered Mr Hri Kumar's suggestion back in 2013 for the Government to introduce a Public Defender scheme to help indigent citizens who face criminal proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Mohamed Irshad asked if we can equip micro enterprises with legal resources, such as business contract templates.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This would, no doubt, simplify the process and the way in which legal services may be delivered on simple matters, but it is probably more appropriate for the Law Society to take this on and we will consult with the Law Society’s Pro Bono Service Office and other volunteer groups to consider if they can provide the micro enterprises with such assistance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will end off by highlighting the holistic help which some Members have asked about it, in particular Mr Patrick Tay, that LAB and its partners have been giving to legal aid recipients who have more than just legal needs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This addresses Mr Patrick Tay's question about giving such help to families in need, and also Mr Mohamed Irshad's question on public education and what more can be done to bring awareness of these schemes to the public's attention.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members would know that the Ministry works with partners, such as the Law Society and the Community Justice Centre, to raise awareness of the law and avenues of legal help, for example, through pamphlets that are produced and also the annual Law Awareness Weeks.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Law Awareness Weeks, which just took place a few weeks ago, has expanded from one which lasts just one afternoon on one weekend, to one that lasts six weeks and is held at various locations across Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This helps to bring awareness of the offerings that pro bono lawyers working with Law Society can offer to the community.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: LAB is working with other agencies, such as Biglove and Hearts @ Feiyue, for applicants with child protection issues.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The referral protocols allow LAB to refer applicants who require other social services to these agencies for help.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Conversely, the agencies may refer applicants who require legal services to LAB for legal help as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The referrals have helped a number of individuals and I would just like to highlight a few examples.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For one such referral, the applicant had applied for aid for his divorce proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: His wife was verbally and physically abusive to the family on a daily basis, which had a negative impact on the children.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: LAB, when they came to know about this, referred the case to PAVE and worked with PAVE to make arrangements to assign a social worker to the applicant, and also to give counselling to him and his family.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In another case, an 80-year-old applicant had a Personal Protection Order (PPO) and partial Domestic Exclusion Order against his adult son who was violent to him; and this allowed the son to occupy only one room of the flat.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, his son continued to use violence against him and, during one quarrel, his son pushed him on his chest, causing him to hit his back and fracture his rib.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: LAB was aware of this and immediately referred him to PAVE, a family violence specialist agency.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: PAVE worked with the Senior Activity Centre near the applicant's flat to set up a community watch for this individual.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: PAVE then subsequently also worked with LAB to support the applicant throughout the Court process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Where relevant, LAB also proactively assists vulnerable victims and applicants to protect their legal rights.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, if an applicant applies only for assistance in divorce proceedings, but when they come to LAB and LAB officers detect that there might also be family violence involved, then LAB will consider if it would be appropriate for him or her to also commence PPO proceedings or other such measures and assist with those applications.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If the order involves the maintenance of wife and children, we will also inform the applicant how he or she can enforce the order if the other party does not comply with the order.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would just like to make a few remarks in conclusion.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, to thank the Members' support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Bill will allow the LAB to continue its good work.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is part and parcel of MinLaw's efforts to ensure that legal representation remains accessible for the general public and, in particular, the most vulnerable of persons.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Beyond legal aid, MinLaw is also committed to ensuring that the legal process is made simple and that access to justice in other forms will be enhanced.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we enhance the family justice system, which centres on the welfare of the child and the family, through the Family Justice Review Committee established with MSF and the Courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, we are also looking at substantive reforms in civil law to keep legal costs affordable, to reduce the complexity of civil proceedings and to strengthen the enforcement of civil judgments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We thank them for their continued support, and we will continue to work closely with the legal fraternity to provide access to justice to persons with limited means through pro bono efforts or low bono efforts and assess how we may better recognise lawyers for these efforts, as Ms Rahayu Mahzam had suggested.
